title: Koko Eating Bananas
statement: Koko has `piles` of bananas and `h` hours. Each hour she picks one pile and eats up to `k` bananas from it (if the pile has fewer, she finishes it and waits). Return the **smallest** eating speed `k` that lets her finish every pile within `h` hours.

example.why: At speed 4 the piles take 1 + 2 + 2 + 3 = 8 hours. At speed 3 they would take 10.

picture: Picture trying out eating speeds instead of searching a list. Speeds come in order: if one speed finishes in time, every faster speed does too. So guess the speed in the middle of the possible range and work out how many hours it would take. Too slow? Only faster speeds are worth trying. Fast enough? Keep it in mind and see whether a slower one also works. Each guess halves the range.
idea: We are not searching the array — we are searching for a **number**: the speed `k`, somewhere between 1 and the largest pile.
Speeds have a clear order: if speed `k` is fast enough, every faster speed is too; if it is too slow, every slower speed is too. That *no, no, no, yes, yes, yes* pattern is what binary search needs.

Test the middle speed by adding up the hours for every pile: pile ÷ k, **rounded up**, because part of an hour still uses the whole hour. Too slow → search the faster half. Fast enough → remember it and search the slower half.

say.1: LeetCode puts every answer inside a class named `Solution`. It is only a wrapper: the real work happens in the function below it.
say.2: The function we must write. It gets the banana `piles` and the hours `h`, and returns the slowest speed that still finishes in time.
say.3: The answer lies between 1 banana an hour and the biggest pile (eating faster than that never helps).
say.5: Repeat until the range has shrunk to a single speed.
say.6: Try the speed in the middle of the range.
say.7: The hours needed at that speed. For each pile, `(pile + mid - 1) // mid` is the pile divided by the speed, *rounded up*, because part of an hour still uses a whole hour. `sum` adds them up.
say.9: Does that take more hours than she has?
say.10: Too slow: only faster speeds can work, so the range now starts just above `mid`.
say.12: Fast enough: `mid` might be the answer, but a slower speed might work too. Keep `mid` and drop everything faster.
say.14: The range is down to one speed: the slowest one that is fast enough.

complexity.timeWhy: log m speeds are tested (m = largest pile), and each test adds up all n piles.
complexity.spaceWhy: Only a few numbers are stored.

steps.text: Our example: **`piles = [3,6,7,11], h = 8`**. Each step runs one highlighted line of the code.
The answer is a speed between 1 and 11 (the biggest pile — eating faster than that never helps). Slow speeds fail and fast speeds work, so we can **binary-search the speed**.
